World.title: Man airlifted with life-threatening injuries after caravan park brawl
World.content:
A man has been airlifted to hospital with life-threatening injuries after being stabbed during a wild brawl at a caravan park in a small Victorian town.

Officers attended the park in the town of Merrigum, about 25 kilometres from Shepparton, after receiving several reports about a brawl involving knives, about 3:45am today.

"When police arrived, they found several people who were believed to be alcohol-affected walking throughout the park and a critically injured man inside one of the cabins," a Victoria Police statement said.

The injured man, a 30-year-old from the local area, was treated by paramedics before being flown to hospital.

Two men were arrested nearby, with police also seizing a knife from the scene.

Shepparton Crime Investigation Unit detectives will interview the men, who were a 28-year-old from Cootamundra, New South Wales, and a 51-year-old from Merrigum.

Anyone who witnessed the brawl or has information should contact Crime Stoppers via crimestoppersvic.com.au or on 1800 333 000.

World.title: Israeli police video shows attack on nun in Jerusalem
World.content:
Israeli police have released video showing what eyewitnesses have said was an attack by a Jewish man on a nun near Jerusalem's Old City.

Footage showed a man following the nun, pushing her to the ground, briefly walking away, and then returning to beat her as she lay on the ground, before bystanders intervened.

The attack took place near David's Tomb — a holy site outside Zion's Gate on the southern side of the Old City — on Tuesday afternoon.

The date when the video was recorded was verified by an official statement from the Israeli Foreign Ministry, which said that the attack occurred on April 28.

The Ministry's statement on X said: "This shameful act stands in direct contradiction to the values of respect, coexistence, and religious freedom upon which Israel is founded and to which it remains deeply committed."

Video, released by police, shows the nun's bruised face. (Supplied: Israeli Police)

Olivier Poquillon, the director of the French School of Biblical and Archaeological Research, said the nun was a researcher at the school.

He called the attack an "act of sectarian violence" in a post on X.

Attacks on Christian communities in East Jerusalem and Israel have been on the rise in recent years, according to the Rossing Center for Education and Dialogue, which tracks such incidents.

Police said the suspect, a 36-year-old man, was later arrested.

In a statement on X, Israel Police said: "In a city sacred to Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike, we remain committed to protecting all communities and ensuring those responsible for violence are held accountable."

Israel also drew international criticism recently after a soldier photographed himself having bludgeoned a fallen statue of Jesus on the cross with what appeared to be an axe in southern Lebanon.

Israeli leaders later disavowed the incident and said he would be reprimanded.

Reuters/AP

World.title: Engineering students launch rocket to 10,000 feet in Australian outback
World.content:
Students with space industry aspirations have been venturing to far west New South Wales to send their skills skyward.

While Artemis II was floating around in space, the University of Sydney's (USYD) student rocketry team took a 12-hour road journey to a sheep station between Mildura and Broken Hill.

They brought with them components for a sounding rocket named Galah.



They had to meticulously reassemble it upon arrival, with the aim of sending it 10,000 feet (3,048 metres) in the air.

Sounding rocket Galah successfully launched 10,000 feet in the air earlier this month. (Supplied: USYD Rocketry Team)

Students designed every component of the projectile, and the closer they got it to their target altitude, the better their performance was judged to be.

Outback rocket launching

The USYD Rocketry Team has been going to Tolarno Station every Easter since 2022.

About 90 students spend months involved in a project where a rocket named after an Australian bird is designed, manufactured and tinkered with.

All parts of the rocket launch were transported to far west New South Wales. (Supplied: USYD Rocketry Team)

The squad also decides what altitude to target in feet, with previous teams having success reaching peak heights of 10,000 and 30,000 feet.

Project manager Michael Bogeholz said it was not only mechanical, aerospace and mechatronic engineering students who participated.

"We get people from all sample areas of the uni, from arts majors to science majors to computer science majors to help put this rocket together," Mr Bogeholz said.

Putting together the rockets takes months of student effort. (Supplied: USYD Rocketry Team)

"Not only do we have a technical side but we have an operations side which handles our finances, business, media and sponsorships."

The university has a facility between Sydney and Canberra where the components designed each year can be tested, but nothing matches the thrill, adrenaline rush and tension of launch week in the outback.

The trek to Tolarno Station is about outcomes.

The propulsion, flight systems, payload, modelling and ground support teams launch the rocket twice in a week (weather permitting) to validate their hard work, and seek repeatable results.

Eyes on the skies

The rocketry program has seen a shift in its participant credentials and leadership opportunities in recent years.

"In 2022 the majority of our team members were in their late years, third or fourth year, but as of now in our current project, a lot of members are in first, second and third year," Mr Bogeholz said.

Among those who have upskilled and taken on leadership opportunities is Lillie Mellin.

Lillie Mellin says the launch is a great opportunity for students. (Supplied: USYD Rocketry Team)

She is a fifth-year student, studying a Bachelor of Mechatronic Engineering and a Bachelor of Law.

She is the systems engineer for the Galah project, having had previous roles as a senior engineer and in ground control.

"It's hands-on and technically so much more demanding than other experiences at uni, so you're just forced to learn so much," Ms Mellin said.

"It's been a really good insight into how engineering works in the real world, which we try and follow as closely as we possibly can as a student team."

Charlie Balderstone is a third-year Mechatronic Engineering student and is the technical director of the Galah project.

Charlie Balderstone prepares the internal components of Galah ahead of launch. (Supplied: USYD Rocketry Team)

He helped lead a team of 27 people to a successful launch sequence.

"We're split across a range of disciplines, from electronics to control the rocket, structures, to make any repairs that need to happen, and propulsion fluids people," he said.

"Back in Sydney we've got about 60. There's a lot of people back closer to home listening in on all the information we can give them from out here.

" Obviously it's cool to watch a rocket go up and it is 10 times cooler when it is something that you've put together. "

The sky isn't the limit

Once the outback launch week has wrapped up, the team must consider who to send to the International Rocket Engineering Competition with the Galah rocket.

It is an event where student rocketry teams from across the globe converge, aiming to get as close to their target altitudes as possible within their various categories.

Three University of Sydney students carry Galah to its launch rail. (Supplied: USYD Rocketry Team)

The USYD team has entered the 10,000ft Student Researched and Developed Hybrid/Liquid competition.

They will be up against a team from RMIT University in Melbourne, as well as four American, one Canadian and one Turkish university teams.

Galah is the USYD rocketry team's fourth rocket aiming for 10,000 feet.

Charlie Balderstone secures a parachute to Galah. (Supplied: USYD Rocketry Team)

Two of their previous efforts have won international competitions.

Pardalote came first last year in its category after it reached 10,342 feet (3,152m), and Silvereye came first as well in 2019, reaching 10,027 feet (3,056m).

The Galah rocket managed a peak height of 10,200 feet (3,108m) during its launch at Tolarno Station.

Space career opportunities

Mr Balderstone said he was confident the skills learnt through the rocketry program gave students the best opportunity to enter the Australian space industry.

"These competitions want to see that we have a very in-depth understanding of every part of the system and that understanding is hard to come by, even in industry," Mr Balderstone said.

"They are primarily about how accurately you can simulate the rocket, how accurately you can make sure it slows down in time to hit that 10,000-foot number right on the dot.

"By targeting that through the student level of the workforce, you're setting up very well for the future of engineers in Australia."

Flight systems lead Riley Smith works with Lillie Mellin on the final assembly. (Supplied: USYD Rocketry Team)

Ms Mellin said the experience had made her realise her passion lay in the engineering component of her degree.

"Since joining rocketry, that's kind of opened my eyes to that side of engineering and those kind of industries," she said.

"[I'm] definitely leaning towards the engineering portion, with law kind of assisting my engineering degree with those soft skills."

World.title: Ghost rainbows, storms and sunsets — WA's skies, captured by you
World.content:
April delivered a classic autumnal mix of warm beach weather and cool, wet days as we head into winter.

From storms to stunning sunsets, we look back at some of the spectacular photographs sent in by ABC readers from across the state.

North vs South

It was a calm start to the month in Western Australia, with the state's split weather personality on full display.

While the northern half baked under the warm sun, the south was blanketed by cloud which produced rain in some parts.

A sunrise at Lake Ballard in the Goldfields. (Supplied: Steve Hutchins)

Perth felt the temperature extremes over the Easter long weekend, reaching a mostly sunny 29 degrees Celsius on Good Friday and dropping to 18.6C by Monday, the perfect excuse to stay in with tea and leftover chocolate.

Star Swamp in North Beach in Perth on Good Friday morning. (Supplied: Neil Treasure )

Chilly mornings

As April went on, the overnight lows gradually dropped.

Rowers along the Canning River braved a chilly 9.8 degree morning on April 8 to squeeze in some exercise at the crack of dawn.

Rowers glide over the Canning River on a cool morning. (Supplied: Sylvia Backer)

It was one of a handful of mornings that got below 10 degrees.

The morning of April 22 will be one to remember for folks in Newdegate and Wandering who woke to a frosty minimum below one degree.

Perth also experienced its coldest morning since October, dropping to just 7.2 degrees.

There were also notable cool maximum temperatures in April, with Swanbourne reaching a record low April maximum of 16.4C, and the Perth Metro having its second-coldest April day at the Mount Lawley site with a temperature of 16.8C.

Despite the brisk weather, we received plenty of impressive sunrise photos.

Surfers enjoy a spectacular sunrise in Exmouth. (Supplied: Naomi Mallin)

Swimmers flock to Avalon Beach in Mandurah at dawn. (Supplied: Leonie Birch)

Dry first half for Perth

The second week of April was pleasant, with summer-like conditions sticking around for much of the south.

It was lovely beach weather for one of our viewers, Andy Burrows, who enjoyed the sunset with his dog Loki.

Loki strikes a pose at sunset at Yallingup Beach. (Supplied: Andy Burrows)

With no rain recorded in Perth for the first fortnight, the mostly sunny days made for an optimal time to explore the verdant Perth Hills.

Sunlight and clouds above Wungong in the Perth Hills. (Supplied: Stephen Thomas)

The settled autumn weather prompted authorities to conduct their usual prescribed burns for Perth and parts of the south.

While there were smoke warnings for some areas of the state, the haze made for colourful sunrises, enjoyed here by Jane Spurgeon and her aptly named pup Ember.

The sun rises over Busselton in mid-April. (Supplied: Jane Spurgeon)

Storms arrive

The middle of the month marked a distinct change in the weather, after a trough along the west coast became active, producing thunderstorms on Wednesday, April 14.

It was the first burst of rainfall for Perth for the month, and it came hard and fast, most of it falling in an hour between 6:30am and 7.30am.

The storm was captured dramatically here by Ryan O’Connell, who was flying from Jandakot to Cue when the sky put on a light show.

Lightning cracks around a plane travelling from Jandakot to Cue. (Supplied: Ryan O'Connell)

The rain from those storms added to the wettest day for the month, which was in the 24 hours to 9am on April 15, when 11.6mm fell.

Then came a series of cold fronts moving through the state’s South West, marking the start of a more active rain season.

The first major storm brought winds exceeding 100 kilometres an hour, leaving a trail of damage throughout southern WA, with a roof ripped off a house in Bunbury and multiple other properties reporting damage.

A roof has been ripped off this house in East Bunbury during a storm on Monday night. (ABC South West WA: Madigan Landry)

The Bureau of Meteorology said there was not enough evidence to conclusively determine if the powerful system was a tornado or microburst.

The fronts that followed didn’t pack the same punch but dumped enough rain to give the lawns a decent drink.

Meanwhile further east, the Goldfields and Esperance regions were also putting on a dramatic show, with storms firing off.

A storm over Lucky Bay in Esperance. (Supplied: Sharn Trutt )

The rainfall brought Esperance to a monthly total of 65.6 millimetres, nearly double its average rainfall for April.

Meanwhile Laverton recorded more than triple its average with just a handful of rainy days totalling 62.8mm.

Sunset at Window Rock in Green Head in the Mid West. (Supplied: John Koch )

Taking stock of the total rain in the first two months of autumn — spanning March and April — we've had 110.4mm so far, which is almost double the 56.2mm long-term average.

Rainbows and fogbows

We were also treated to some lovely shots of the rainbows that followed the light drizzles in Perth, and a rare ghostly white 'fogbow'.

A rainbow over Brighton Beach in Perth. (Supplied)

A fogbow in Tenterden in the Great Southern. (Supplied: Elly Landridge)

After a week of cold fronts shaking things up, conditions settled over the ANZAC Day long weekend.

We had some crisp temperatures around for the dawn service, but the sun quickly warmed things up during the day.

Sunrise in Albany for the ANZAC Day dawn service. (Supplied: Tania Wood )

Before we had the chance to fully appreciate the sunny weather over the weekend, we were thrown back into the cold and wet conditions.

A trough and large cloud band dragged tropical moisture across a big chunk of the state, producing showers and storms across western and southern parts.

Lower King in Albany shrouded in thick fog. (Supplied: Clodagh Irwin )

The rainfall helped push Perth above its long-term April rainfall average, with the city now sitting at a healthy 37.8mm.

And on the last day of April, Perth and the South West Land Division woke up to a very foggy morning resulting from high moisture, low overnight temperatures and light winds, according to the Bureau of Meteorology.

The CBD was shrouded in fog on Thursday, which cleared by about 10am. (Supplied: Jasper Reid)

If you have a great weather photo you'd like to see featured in ABC Perth's 7PM News or online, send them through to Tabarak at waweather@abc.net.au.

World.title: Live: Lions disappointed after whiteboard analysis on Bombers is leaked
World.content:
An image has been leaked on social media showing the Brisbane Lions' pre-match analysis of their Essendon opponents.

The drama has overshadowed the Lions' commanding 64-point win over the Bombers at Docklands.

Later, West Coast hosts Richmond in Perth, and Geelong faces North Melbourne at Kardinia Park.

The Saturday action wraps up in the evening, when Carlton plays St Kilda at Docklands.

Follow the live blog below, keep up to date with all the latest stats in our ScoreCentre, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

Reader reaction to whiteboard drama L By Luke Pentony Really disgusting Social Media post of a whiteboard notes on Essendon Bombers players very insulting that’s for sure catch this person please! - Christiane Meanwhile … L By Luke Pentony We'll keep you across the upcoming two matches, while also report on reaction from the coach media conferences following the Lions vs Bombers match. 'Obviously disappointing' L By Luke Pentony Lions co-captain Josh Dunkley has also spoken about the leaked image of the whiteboard. It probably shouldn't say weaknesses on there, " Dunkley told Fox Footy after the match. It's obviously disappointing that inside the four walls something has leaked out of the inner sanctum. But that's footy. We know we're under the microscope every day … we've obviously got to learn from the experience. Zorko speaks about whiteboard notes L By Luke Pentony Dayne Zorko has spoken to ABC Sport after the match, addressing the image of the whiteboard notes that has circulated on social media. It is believed the image was taken by the parent of an Auskick participant at the Lions' training headquarters. We were made aware of that last night. We were really obviously disappointed that we allow external programs to come in and use our state-of-the-art facilities. It was probably harmless … it’s not new for us, we’ve done an opposition board for a number of years, ever since Fages (coach Chris Fagan) has been at our football club. We want to know a little bit more about our opposition. We’re obviously really disappointed with that, but we put that to bed this morning, and we got to work. Zorko added: The game's way too hard to be worrying about what was said on a whiteboard. I don't think there was anything too derogatory towards anyone, [it] just gives us a better understanding of the opposition we're coming up against. Establishing their command from the opening minute, the Lions have cruised to a comfortable 22.11 (143) to 11.13 (79) victory over the Bombers. The home side showed fight at times, especially in the final term, but the Lions' win was never in doubt. They move to a 5-3 win-loss record, while the Bombers are 1-7. Cox on target for Bombers L By Luke Pentony Nik Cox is found on his own inside the Bombers' attacking 50. He kicks truly for a deserved goal, but the Lions still lead by more than 60 points as full-time approaches. Cameron gets a double L By Luke Pentony Charlie Cameron feasts on a Bombers turnover to record his second goal. The Lions grabbed back possession from the Bombers and quickly transferred the ball to Cameron, who did the rest. Lohmann joins Morris with a fourth L By Luke Pentony Kai Lohmann is awarded a free kick inside the attacking 50. He shows impressive accuracy from in front of the sticks to kick his fourth goal of the contest. Four goals to Morris L By Luke Pentony Logan Morris adds to his goal tally, taking a contested mark before landing his set-shot with ease. The Lions lead by 57 points with just over five minutes remaining in the match. Langford finally on the board for Bombers L By Luke Pentony Kyle Langford kicked two behinds earlier in the match, but he now has a goal to his name late in the final quarter. He continues the Bombers' fightback, even if it won't prevent the Lions from grabbing the four competition points. McKenna responds for Lions L By Luke Pentony Any celebrations for Nate Caddy's third goal would have ended abruptly, with Conor McKenna replying for the Lions. McKenna now has two goals for the visitors. Caddy kicks his third for the match L By Luke Pentony Nate Caddy marks on the lead in the pocket, before slotting his third goal. The Bombers deserve praise for not giving up, but the Lions still hold a commanding lead. They're up for 51 points. Lions find a reply L By Luke Pentony After three straight Bombers goals, the Lions stem the tide through Bruce Reville. Reville's major has the Lions leading by 56 points midway through the final term. Bombers kick a third straight goal L By Luke Pentony Peter Wright has a second goal for the Bombers, cutting back the Lions' lead to 49 points. Bombers snare another major L By Luke Pentony Bombers youngster Sullivan Robey does well to navigate defensive traffic after a stoppage and slot a goal. It's back-to-back majors for the Bombers, but the Lions lead by 55 points. Merrett gives Bombers reason to cheer … sort of L By Luke Pentony The Bombers are showing fight already in the fourth quarter, with Zach Merrett getting the first goal of the term. It's a positive start for the Bombers, but they have a mountain to climb in the final term. Fourth quarter gets underway L By Luke Pentony The final term has made a start at Docklands, with the Lions leading by 69 points. Show more posts

World.title: Cosmetics will soon cost more. Here's why
World.content:
Australians will likely be forced to pay more for cosmetic products, such as lipsticks and moisturisers, due to crude oil supply disruptions caused by the Middle East war.

Even if the situation stabilises soon, higher prices for petroleum-derived raw materials have already flowed through and will take months to normalise, an industry expert warns.

In Australia, the beauty and personal care market is expected to earn more than $12 billion in revenue in 2026, according to market data company Statista.

Iran war live updates: For the latest news on the Middle East crisis, read our blog.

On average, Australians spend about $454 per year on products, but it could soon get a lot higher.

Let's break it down.

The battle over the Strait of Hormuz By moving so much of the war into the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf, Tehran has hit its adversaries where it hurts the most and analysts warn that while the United States military is mighty, history shows in asymmetrical warfare, the lesser power can win the day.

First, how are oil and cosmetics connected?

Apart from its crucial role in energy and logistics, oil — also referred to as petroleum or crude oil — is a key component in many commonly used cosmetic products including lipsticks, skincare and even conditioner.

However, you are not just spreading crude oil on your lips.

It takes a complex multi-step process to turn crude oil into cosmetic products, says Sebastien Jagut, the procurement and business development manager at New Directions Australia, a manufacturer and wholesaler of cosmetic products.

Australian dependence on imported packaging exposed by Iran war The war in Iran renews the government's interest in reducing Australia's dependence on imported packaging, particularly oil-reliant plastic.

In simple terms, crude oil, after extraction, is refined into petrochemical derivatives that require further chemical processing to become cosmetic ingredients.

These raw materials include:

Glycerine

Petroleum jelly (petrolatum)

Mineral oil (paraffin oil)

Silicones

Glycols

Polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)

These components are typically used to create beauty products because they are cheap, stable and create a glossy texture.

Vaseline ointment is made of 100 per cent purified petroleum jelly. (ABC News: Yiying Li)

For example, Vaseline — a topical ointment used to trap your skin's existing moisture — is 100 per cent purified petroleum jelly.

Are you paying more for your cosmetic items? We would like to hear from you! Contact our journalist confidentially on li.yiying@abc.net.au or li.yiying@proton.me.

Cosmetics manufacturers feeling the pinch

Fuel shortages and rising energy costs are already impacting the price and availability of those raw materials, says Mr Jagut.

The price of raw materials in many commonly used beauty products has already increased. (ABC News: Nicholas Martyr)

"In addition, we are seeing freight surcharges introduced by distributors in Australia, reflecting the increased cost of transporting goods into the country," he said.

"Given Australia's reliance on imported raw materials, this adds significant pressure across the supply chain.

"Beyond pricing, the real concern is supply continuity — delays, reduced availability, and longer lead times are becoming increasingly likely."

Price of groceries to increase within weeks due to war in Iran Farmers ask for a 30-cent-per-litre price rise for milk as fuel and fertiliser prices surge.

Could it lead to more 'clean' beauty products?

Amina Kitching, the founder of LOAEL global beauty group, which is a beauty educator, researcher and advocate for organic beauty standards, says the petroleum shortage is creating a "perfect storm" for Australia's cosmetics industry.

"[It is] leading to significantly higher production costs, supply chain bottlenecks, and a potential, immediate, or near-future shortage of finished goods," Ms Kitching said.

" The cost of raw materials and plastic packaging [polyethylene] has hit record highs, making the production of lipstick, creams and plastic containers significantly more expensive. "

What lipstick sales tell us about the economy There are renewed warnings of dark clouds hanging over the Australian economy, reinforced by the increase in sales of lipstick.

She added that cosmetics companies were passing increased costs to consumers, with price hikes for both raw ingredients and finished packaged goods expected soon.

Ms Kitching said she hoped the price hikes would push the industry toward "greater adoption of sustainable alternatives".

"[It is] a welcome shift away from the 'throwaway' culture towards more sustainable and reusable packaging options," she said.

" People need to learn to live without petrochemicals. "

What's next for cosmetics prices?

Mr Jagut from New Directions Australia said that historically, during periods of inflation, the personal care sector was among the first to feel the impact.

Sebastien Jagut says cosmetic businesses are already facing higher prices. (Supplied: New Directions Australia)

"Consumers tend to prioritise essential spending — food, fuel, health care — which can reduce demand for discretionary products like cosmetics," he said.

"This creates a double pressure: rising production costs and potentially softening demand."

Mr Jagut said there were clear early signs of caution for businesses.

"New product launches are being delayed, new market entrants are hesitating, [and] brands are becoming more conservative in their planning due to cost uncertainty."

Apart from higher costs, he warned consumers in Australia would likely face shortages of certain items and reduced product variety.

World.title: WA’s first set of quadruplets in six years delivered in Perth hospital
World.content:
NationalWABabies WA’s first set of quadruplets in six years delivered in Perth hospital Rebecca Peppiatt May 2, 2026 — 4:02pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

WA’s first set of quadruplets in six years were delivered at King Edward Memorial Hospital on Tuesday, surprising their Kalgoorlie parents who already have a three-year-old son. Belinda and Emmanuel Lotsu thought they were having triplets after a successful IVF journey last year. Belinda and Emmanuel Lotsu with two of their four newborns. North Metropolitan Health Service But halfway through the pregnancy, were told there were actually four babies on the way. “You could see the surprise on her face,” Emmanuel told 9 News Perth. “She was so surprised and stunned.”



The babies - three girls and a boy - were delivered via cesarean section on Tuesday at 32 weeks and three days, ranging in weight from 1.5 to 2 kilograms. “She’s done absolutely amazing getting them to 33 weeks for four babies, growing at the rate that they did,” King Edward Memorial Hospital Nurse and Midwifery Coordinator Jourdin Ross said. Belinda Lotsu was surprised to find out she was having four babies. North Metropolitan Health Service “They’re all doing exceptionally well. World.title: Trump has a new target in Europe – and there is a price for speaking up
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeMiddle East at war Trump has a new target in Europe – and there is a price for speaking up David Crowe May 2, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: When dealing with Donald Trump, speaking your mind can come at a cost. So German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is being blasted by the US president after revealing his thoughts about the war with Iran. Merz, a conservative who usually avoids clashing with Trump, declared on Monday that America was being “humiliated” by Iran and had no clear way out of the conflict. Friedrich Merz drives an armoured fighting vehicle during a visit to the Bundeswehr base in Munster on Thursday. AP Trump, clearly furious on social media, threatened retaliation. But rather than resorting to tariffs, his preferred tool in the past, he raised the idea of withdrawing US troops from German bases they have used for decades. Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of war, followed up within a day. He moved on Friday afternoon in Washington (early on Saturday, AEST) to remove an army brigade from Germany, or about 5000 troops, over the next year. He is also reported to be halting a plan from the Biden administration to deploy a battalion to Germany with long-range conventional missiles.



Suddenly, a foundation stone of the Western alliance is in doubt. No country in Europe has more American troops than Germany. With 49,000 military and civilian personnel, the country has more American defence service members on active duty than many US states. The Pentagon changes appear to have been in the works for months, so they are not happening simply because the German chancellor spoke up. Trump has complained about troop numbers in Germany for years, including in his first term as president, and now sees a chance to do something. US President Donald Trump in Florida on Friday. AP Even so, the timing suggests that the frank talk in Germany made Trump more eager to act. And the defence decision came when the president slapped higher tariffs on European cars, also hurting Germany. Merz angered Trump because he lanced the presidential hyperbole about the war.



“The Iranians are clearly stronger than expected, and the Americans clearly have no truly convincing strategy in the negotiations either,” the chancellor said to students at an event in Marburg. “The problem with conflicts like this is always: you don’t just have to get in, you have to get out again. We saw that very painfully in Afghanistan for 20 years. We saw it in Iraq. A soldier from the US Army uses a DroneShield counter-drone gun during the Combined Resolve “Greywolves” exercise in Hohenfels, Germany, on Thursday. Bloomberg “At the moment, I do not see what strategic exit the Americans will choose, especially since the Iranians are clearly negotiating very skilfully – or very skilfully not negotiating.” His conclusion: “A whole nation is being humiliated by the Iranian leadership.”



European leaders know to expect retaliation from the White House. Trump has already warned that he could withdraw the US from the NATO alliance, though he would have to gain approval from Congress for this drastic step. In practical terms, his disputes with NATO already weaken the pact. Related Article Middle East at war This man negotiated the last Iran deal. He reveals the ‘secret sauce’ needed now Germany’s own actions show that it is preparing for a time when it has less support from across the Atlantic. And it is not alone. French President Emmanuel Macron has talked to Merz about a joint European nuclear deterrent to fill the American security gap. France has the fourth-largest nuclear arsenal in the world. Merz is already spending heavily on defence in the knowledge that Germany will have to do more without American help. Germany was the largest military spender among European NATO members last year, lifting its outlays by 24 per cent to $US114 billion (about $160 billion). A new report from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute notes that this is only 2.3 per cent of GDP, but the German economy is the third largest in the world when measured in US dollars. “In 2025, military spending by European NATO members rose faster than at any time since 1953,” said Jade Guiberteau Ricard, a researcher at the institute.



The next German budget is expected to lift defence spending to about 3.7 per cent of GDP by 2030, even though this means taking on debt. (This is the strategic background to Australia’s growing defence relationship with Germany.) Merz wants Germany to have the biggest army in Europe, though he confronts popular concern. A new law has cleared the way for conscription if the country cannot add 20,000 personnel with volunteers alone. Some of the younger generation think Merz and his government are asking too much. A US Air Force cargo plane takes off from Ramstein Air Base in April. Getty Images The spending increases will continue across Europe, and not just because Trump complains that the spending has been too low. European leaders are adjusting to a world in which America is less reliable. Trump’s waning interest in Ukraine has been the obvious signal of this. The troop withdrawal from Germany amplifies it. The Hegseth announcement needs to be put into perspective. The US has withdrawn troops from Germany in the past. The 49,000 personnel in Germany at the end of December was slightly higher than the 47,000 at the end of 2015, according to public data from the Defence Manpower Data Centre, or DMDC. But it was down from 58,000 in 2010.



How did that happen? Barack Obama, the US president seen as a staunch friend of Europe, withdrew two combat brigades from Germany in 2012, amounting to about 7000 troops. The NATO pact survived this shift in force posture because the numbers are not the greatest challenge here. The biggest problem is that Trump does not believe in NATO, the alliance that won the Cold War. Other European leaders know they could be in for the same treatment. Trump has widened his complaints in the past few days to suggest that he could order US troops out of Italy and Spain, given he thinks they have not helped in the war with Iran. “Yeah, I probably will,” he said when asked about this in the Oval Office. “Italy has not been of any help, and Spain has been horrible.” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez opposes the war and refuses to allow US aircraft to use Spanish bases to launch attacks on Iran. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni stopped US forces using an air base in Sicily in March.



Even so, Italy and Spain support thousands of US personnel at army, navy and air force bases. And the US forces are not there to defend Italy and Spain; their primary purpose is to defend America. Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war It’s easy for Trump to weaken NATO but pulling out of the pact is a lot harder The DMDC reports show there were more than 15,000 active US defence personnel – military and civilian – in Italy in December, and about 4300 in Spain. There were just over 11,500 in Britain. (For all of Trump’s interest in Greenland, there were only 137 on the Arctic territory.) All this military muscle is there to ensure Trump, or another president, can project American power at great distance from the White House. And that means that withdrawing too many of these assets will weaken US capacity.



None of this means Europe can defend itself easily without America. The big winner from a substantial American withdrawal would be Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I think Putin will love it,” said NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in January, when a European Parliament committee asked him about this scenario. Related Article Foreign relations Hegseth notes Australia’s defence spending hike, says there’s more to do Rutte warned that Europe would suffer an immense burden if it had to fill the gap left by a US retreat. “And if anyone thinks here, again, that the European Union, or Europe as a whole, can defend itself without the US, keep on dreaming,” he told the parliamentarians. “You can’t. We can’t. We need each other.” Rutte, one of the closest friends Trump has in Europe, is always more optimistic about the alliance than others. But he was also being coolly rational. For the Americans to remain safe, he said, they need a secure Arctic, a secure North Atlantic and a secure Europe.



“So, the US has every interest in NATO, as much as Canada and the European NATO allies,” he said. Trump can withdraw a brigade from Germany, as Obama did. But he would have to think twice about a sweeping withdrawal of ships, aircraft and troops from Europe. In the meantime, he won’t think twice about making the threat. World.title: Teen star reveals why he knocked back Gus and rugby ahead of date with Cleary
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 Teen star reveals why he knocked back Gus and rugby ahead of date with Cleary Adrian Proszenko Updated May 2, 2026 — 3:55pm ,first published 12:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To fully appreciate the hype around teenage Manly halfback Joey Walsh, who makes his starting NRL debut against Penrith champion Nathan Cleary on Sunday, consider that he has already knocked back overtures from Phil Gould and dealt with predictions he would be the Wallabies five-eighth for the Rugby World Cup had he stuck with the 15-man code. It’s not quite the hype that met Lachlan Galvin’s entry into the big time, but it’s not far off. Joey Walsh will make his NRL run-on debut against Nathan Cleary on Sunday. Peter Rae A groin injury has ruled regular Sea Eagles No.7 Jamal Fogarty out of the Sea Eagles’ clash with the Panthers at CommBank Stadium, resulting in a long-awaited elevation for Walsh. At the age of 19, with just 19 minutes of first-grade experience – he made his debut off the bench against the Warriors in the final game of last season – Walsh is tasked with marking the Panthers maestro. It is a mammoth task, but good judges have always felt he was destined for big things.



Earlier this year, Panthers legend Greg Alexander waxed lyrical after closely observing Walsh play rugby for St Augustine’s College in Brookvale. “I thought he’s as good as any kid I’ve ever seen at schoolboy level,” Alexander told SEN radio. Manly interim coach Kieran Foran says Walsh is ready for regular NRL football. Wolter Peeters “If he didn’t sign with Manly, and stayed with Manly [in rugby] where he was signed with the Waratahs, I’ve got no doubt that next year he would be the Wallabies five-eighth.” Ultimately, Walsh chose to switch to the Sea Eagles, and will get an opportunity to show everyone what all the fuss is about.



“It’s a big call, I’m not too sure about all of that,” Walsh said of Alexander’s comments. “Brandy’s a great bloke, I played lots of school footy with his son Beau, who’s a really good player, too. Nice to hear those things, but obviously you don’t want to read into it too much … Our club definitely provides lots of support about not letting it get to your head, so a big focus for me is honestly playing my footy and focusing on footy when I’m at training. Loading “But I’m taking a step away from it at home, trying not to look into social media too much because whether it’s good or bad, it’s not gonna do too much good for me, so I just try to stay away from it.” Another admirer is Gould, who tried to poach Walsh before he brought Galvin to Canterbury.



“He was a really great bloke to meet and obviously, he’s running a very successful club over there,” Walsh said of Gould in a recent interview with this masthead. “Hopefully, I’ll stay in contact with him throughout my career, but for me Manly’s a very local club. I grew up here, so it’s pretty exciting to be able to play for a local team.” Joey Walsh will start at halfback for Manly against the Panthers on Sunday night. Sitthixay Ditthavong Manly have earmarked Walsh and fellow young gun Onitoni Large as their long-term halves. Interim Sea Eagles coach Kieran Foran opted not to rush the captain of the Australian under-18s rugby team straight into the side when he first took over from Anthony Seibold, but on Saturday felt he was ready to take on premiership frontrunners Penrith. “He’s got endless natural ability,” Foran said in his pre-game media conference. “On top of that, he is a wonderful student of the game, he works extremely hard. He is a tough kid and is really courageous and competitive.



Related Article NRL 2026 Has the need for speed turned the NRL into touch footy? These numbers suggest otherwise “He just ticks so many boxes. Without putting too much pressure on him, we have high hopes for Joey’s future in this game. We love what he is about. “And tomorrow night he gets to go out there and do it. And we have all the belief in the world he is going to get out there and get the job done.” One of Walsh’s idols growing up was Daly Cherry-Evans. The youngster said he was fortunate to spend time with the former Manly captain while they are both at the club. “I learned loads, he was unreal to me,” Walsh said. “He spent lots of time helping me improve my game, obviously because it was my first year coming back to league.



“He’s taught me to keep playing eyes-up footy, the structure and all that will come with games, but just try and keep your eyes up and play with your instincts, which was a very good lesson.” With AAP

Although Sam Groth is absent from the booths today, many of his former Liberal colleagues have made the trip to Nepean to support their candidate, Anthony Marsh.

Former opposition leader Brad Battin (left), Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and Liberal candidate Anthony Marsh. Wayne Taylor

World.title: Since the 1960s, Denis has framed his customers’ treasures: snake skins, wedding dresses and golden underpants
World.content:
Denis Kosnar, who has framed Melburnians’ lives since he was a boy.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Denis Kosnar is wrangling a 2.6-metre python skin, unfurling the great rolled-up beast and flattening it with clamps and weights. Applying snake oil to one side (or, more accurately, glycerin) and rubbing alcohol to the other, he’s been meticulously working to preserve the skin, some weeks after a woman walked into his shop and pulled it out of her bag. Her relative shot and killed it in Sri Lanka 20 years ago, she said. Denis Kosnar in his quaint and curious Kosnar’s Picture Framing and Mirrors Shop. Jason South Kosnar has been a framer for 61 years – but this is a first. “See, there are the creases there,” he says, tracing a finger over the snake’s scales through his phone screen, “we’re starting to get rid of them.” Seventy-three years ago, his father, John (Jan) Kosnar, started the family framing business, working out of a small shed at Ferny Creek in the Dandenong Ranges.



A Czechoslovakian migrant, he brought over picture framing and gilding skills. Soon enough, 14-year-old Denis was apprenticed in their new shop in Moonee Ponds in Melbourne’s north-west – the family’s first major commercial move. At one time, Kosnar’s supplied most picture framers in Australia and New Zealand, and John was formally recognised as the founder of Australia’s industry for picture frame mouldings (individual frame pieces that are cut to size). A factory and dozens of employees (85, at its height) came and went – before financial troubles in the 1990s forced the business to scale back. What’s left today are two workshops, and a quaint storefront in Ascot Vale, a suburb over from where Kosnar, 75, started. Ye olde signage covers the corner shop’s exterior, proudly declaring “Kosnar’s” from all angles. The bell chimes when you pull on the door’s great, golden handle, and inside, Julie – who has worked for the business a decade – uses a ruler and a cardboard pricing chart (dated 1993) to calculate quotes. There’s no computerising of customer orders here (Kosnar reasons that paper records can go back longer, as computer programs change and documents are lost). Thick record books are instead stuffed into shelving in a back room cluttered with hangers, screws, brackets, glues, tools and a small workbench. “When I first came to work here, it was like walking into Dickens,” Julie says, speaking over soft classical music. She waves off a request to publish her surname, insisting she stays “under the radar”.



Hand-constructed ornate frames and mirrors, many gilded by Denis, take up most of the shop’s surfaces, except for a sliver of red carpet. “We frame an awful lot of things,” Julie says. “You’d be surprised.” There was the wedding dress – a big tulle gown with a beaded bodice and empire waist – and last year, a woman came in with a full-face medical mask, with holes cut into it for the eyes. She was in remission after wearing it during cancer treatment. Julie defers to Kosnar, who brings up those golden underpants they put in a showcase frame a few years ago. “It was a prize for doing something,” he says, “but it’s probably best not to be known what it was for.” For all Kosnar’s years, he can’t choose a favourite project (to do so would be like “choosing a favourite child”) – and Kosnar’s are still not Melbourne’s oldest framers. That title belongs to Jarman, the cavernous counterpart to Kosnar’s curiosity, acquired by artists’ services company Chapman and Bailey in 2014. Founded in 1879 by John Thallon and his brother Thomas, the combined business today operates out of a Willy Wonka-style, multistorey building in Abbotsford in Melbourne’s inner north.



The showroom and gallery is merely the taster before the gilding room, the ornamental room, the mounting room, and the spraying room, where a metres-high curtain of water filters out excess paint. Chapman and Bailey’s Ying Huang is among Australia’s last ornamental specialists using traditional framing techniques. Joe Armao The Jarmans are long gone from the business, but the framers’ legacy remains, particularly in ornamental specialist Ying Huang. Beneath hodgepodge plants and old window mounts hung from the ceiling, she cooks up composite in heavy metal pots, before pressing the material into hand-cast ornamental moulds – the main attraction for owner Mark Chapman, who bought Jarman to keep the practice alive. Huang trained under Tom Whitfield, the last of Jarman Framing’s original ornamental specialists, before he retired in 2020. Nowadays, Jarman stocks a frame dubbed the “Tom special”. “One day I’ll have a frame in my name,” Huang says. On the showroom floor, clientele clearly see the value in Jarman’s craft. Two consultants – one, in a tweed vest with thick, black-rimmed glasses – cling to the side of a suited gentleman, who is weighing up framing options for an oil painting on a video call to his wife. The priciest frames here – all of which are museum-quality – can cost up to $30,000. At Kosnar’s, the maximum price is more like $8000. But when I ask Kosnar what the most valuable item they’ve framed is, his answer isn’t monetary.

World.title: Fuel spike is coming: Relief at bowser not tipped to last
World.content:
The cost of petrol and diesel is set to climb again in coming weeks after Australia’s regional oil prices hit a new wartime high, piling pressure on the federal government to extend its 26¢ cut to the fuel excise beyond the June 30 deadline. Motorists have enjoyed a two-week window of relief at the pump after the US-Iran ceasefire raised hopes of an imminent end to the conflict, spurring a swift fall in crude oil and fuel prices. Fuel prices are set to rise. Louie Douvis But as a series of peace talks foundered, crushing prospects of Middle East energy exports returning to normal any time soon, benchmark oil prices have risen to their highest levels since Iran all but closed the Strait of Hormuz on February 28. On Friday, Australia’s regional oil benchmark, Tapis crude, was trading at $US125 ($174) a barrel, its highest mark since the global energy crisis sparked by the war in Ukraine in 2022, and almost double the $US65 price point underpinning the Australian government’s mid-year budget update.



While prices dropped slightly on overseas markets overnight, international oil bosses are sounding the alarm as stockpiles run down. “A lot of the inventory and spare capacity has been depleted already,” Chevron chief financial officer Eimear Bonner told Bloomberg. “There’s very little of the buffer left.” “The market hasn’t seen the full impact of that yet,” Exxon chief executive Darren Woods told analysts overnight. “There’s more to come if the strait remains closed.” “Markets are not liking what is happening in the Middle East,” said Peter Khoury, a spokesman for the National Roads and Motorists Association. Related Article Visual story

Oil If Australia’s greener than ever, how much oil do we really need? The reality is brutal



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Friday that economic damage from the war would have a “long tail to it”. “We don’t know when this war will end. We don’t know what the consequences will be. We don’t know if the Strait of Hormuz will be open, what the timeframe is, and we know that even if it opened tomorrow,” Albanese said. Albanese has not ruled out extending the fuel excise cut beyond June, and said last month that the government would “examine it at an appropriate time”. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has emphasised the role the cut has played in driving down prices since April, after a 33 per cent jump in petrol prices helped push inflation to 4.6 per cent in March. “This shows how important and how necessary that decision from the government was since we halved the fuel excise,” he said on Wednesday.



While Sydney and Melbourne drivers saw regular unleaded averaging $1.80 and diesel at $2.50 a litre on Friday, those figures are expected to jump within seven to 10 days’ time as the international spike filters through to local service stations. In late March, diesel prices hit a high of $3.10 a litre, while unleaded petrol rose to $2.59 a litre. While price spikes are imminent, pressure on the local fuel supply chain has eased. Previously unpublished government data reveals that panic buying has subsided as petrol and diesel sales have returned to typical levels, after consumption hit a high point in the first week of March. Fuel excise volumes – a key indicator of how much fuel has been sold in the nation as it is charged per litre – surged to a six-year peak in the weeks following February 28, when US President Donald Trump launched his attack on Iran. The spike was driven by a wave of panic buying as motorists and businesses braced for the risk of major price hikes and supply shortfalls.



Related Article Inside Story

Energy Scott was already working late on fuel supply when a call stopped him cold However, demand has plummeted by as much as 20 per cent since early March, signalling that motorists are changing their driving behaviour. Prices have eased and supply has increased since fuel importers procured additional cargoes in March and the government secured agreements with Asian fuel exporters to shore up supply. The number of local service stations without fuel has fallen to less than half the number recorded during the first weeks of the war. Experts attribute the massive fall in fuel demand to people changing their driving behaviour to deal with higher prices, as well as the impact of increased government and industry messaging encouraging motorists to adopt fuel-saving measures, take public transport where possible, and not fill up unnecessarily.



“I would suggest it’s all of the above,” Khoury said. “Sustained periods of really high prices result in people driving less, combining trips and using public transport more.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. A new law has cleared the way for conscription if the country cannot add 20,000 personnel with volunteers alone. Some of the younger generation think Merz and his government are asking too much. A US Air Force cargo plane takes off from Ramstein Air Base in April. Getty Images The spending increases will continue across Europe, and not just because Trump complains that the spending has been too low. European leaders are adjusting to a world in which America is less reliable. Trump’s waning interest in Ukraine has been the obvious signal of this. The troop withdrawal from Germany amplifies it. The Hegseth announcement needs to be put into perspective. The US has withdrawn troops from Germany in the past. The 49,000 personnel in Germany at the end of December was slightly higher than the 47,000 at the end of 2015, according to public data from the Defence Manpower Data Centre, or DMDC. But it was down from 58,000 in 2010.



How did that happen? Barack Obama, the US president seen as a staunch friend of Europe, withdrew two combat brigades from Germany in 2012, amounting to about 7000 troops. The NATO pact survived this shift in force posture because the numbers are not the greatest challenge here. The biggest problem is that Trump does not believe in NATO, the alliance that won the Cold War. Other European leaders know they could be in for the same treatment. Trump has widened his complaints in the past few days to suggest that he could order US troops out of Italy and Spain, given he thinks they have not helped in the war with Iran. “Yeah, I probably will,” he said when asked about this in the Oval Office. “Italy has not been of any help, and Spain has been horrible.” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez opposes the war and refuses to allow US aircraft to use Spanish bases to launch attacks on Iran. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni stopped US forces using an air base in Sicily in March.



Even so, Italy and Spain support thousands of US personnel at army, navy and air force bases. And the US forces are not there to defend Italy and Spain; their primary purpose is to defend America. Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war It’s easy for Trump to weaken NATO but pulling out of the pact is a lot harder The DMDC reports show there were more than 15,000 active US defence personnel – military and civilian – in Italy in December, and about 4300 in Spain. There were just over 11,500 in Britain. (For all of Trump’s interest in Greenland, there were only 137 on the Arctic territory.) All this military muscle is there to ensure Trump, or another president, can project American power at great distance from the White House. And that means that withdrawing too many of these assets will weaken US capacity.



None of this means Europe can defend itself easily without America. The big winner from a substantial American withdrawal would be Russian President Vladimir Putin. “I think Putin will love it,” said NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in January, when a European Parliament committee asked him about this scenario. Related Article Foreign relations Hegseth notes Australia’s defence spending hike, says there’s more to do Rutte warned that Europe would suffer an immense burden if it had to fill the gap left by a US retreat. “And if anyone thinks here, again, that the European Union, or Europe as a whole, can defend itself without the US, keep on dreaming,” he told the parliamentarians. “You can’t. We can’t. We need each other.” Rutte, one of the closest friends Trump has in Europe, is always more optimistic about the alliance than others. But he was also being coolly rational. For the Americans to remain safe, he said, they need a secure Arctic, a secure North Atlantic and a secure Europe.



“So, the US has every interest in NATO, as much as Canada and the European NATO allies,” he said. Trump can withdraw a brigade from Germany, as Obama did. But he would have to think twice about a sweeping withdrawal of ships, aircraft and troops from Europe. In the meantime, he won’t think twice about making the threat. World.title: Teen star reveals why he knocked back Gus and rugby ahead of date with Cleary
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 Teen star reveals why he knocked back Gus and rugby ahead of date with Cleary Adrian Proszenko Updated May 2, 2026 — 3:55pm ,first published 12:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To fully appreciate the hype around teenage Manly halfback Joey Walsh, who makes his starting NRL debut against Penrith champion Nathan Cleary on Sunday, consider that he has already knocked back overtures from Phil Gould and dealt with predictions he would be the Wallabies five-eighth for the Rugby World Cup had he stuck with the 15-man code. It’s not quite the hype that met Lachlan Galvin’s entry into the big time, but it’s not far off. Joey Walsh will make his NRL run-on debut against Nathan Cleary on Sunday. Peter Rae A groin injury has ruled regular Sea Eagles No.7 Jamal Fogarty out of the Sea Eagles’ clash with the Panthers at CommBank Stadium, resulting in a long-awaited elevation for Walsh. At the age of 19, with just 19 minutes of first-grade experience – he made his debut off the bench against the Warriors in the final game of last season – Walsh is tasked with marking the Panthers maestro. It is a mammoth task, but good judges have always felt he was destined for big things.



Earlier this year, Panthers legend Greg Alexander waxed lyrical after closely observing Walsh play rugby for St Augustine’s College in Brookvale. “I thought he’s as good as any kid I’ve ever seen at schoolboy level,” Alexander told SEN radio. Manly interim coach Kieran Foran says Walsh is ready for regular NRL football. Wolter Peeters “If he didn’t sign with Manly, and stayed with Manly [in rugby] where he was signed with the Waratahs, I’ve got no doubt that next year he would be the Wallabies five-eighth.” Ultimately, Walsh chose to switch to the Sea Eagles, and will get an opportunity to show everyone what all the fuss is about.



“It’s a big call, I’m not too sure about all of that,” Walsh said of Alexander’s comments. “Brandy’s a great bloke, I played lots of school footy with his son Beau, who’s a really good player, too. Nice to hear those things, but obviously you don’t want to read into it too much … Our club definitely provides lots of support about not letting it get to your head, so a big focus for me is honestly playing my footy and focusing on footy when I’m at training. Loading “But I’m taking a step away from it at home, trying not to look into social media too much because whether it’s good or bad, it’s not gonna do too much good for me, so I just try to stay away from it.” Another admirer is Gould, who tried to poach Walsh before he brought Galvin to Canterbury.



“He was a really great bloke to meet and obviously, he’s running a very successful club over there,” Walsh said of Gould in a recent interview with this masthead. “Hopefully, I’ll stay in contact with him throughout my career, but for me Manly’s a very local club. I grew up here, so it’s pretty exciting to be able to play for a local team.” Joey Walsh will start at halfback for Manly against the Panthers on Sunday night. Sitthixay Ditthavong Manly have earmarked Walsh and fellow young gun Onitoni Large as their long-term halves. Interim Sea Eagles coach Kieran Foran opted not to rush the captain of the Australian under-18s rugby team straight into the side when he first took over from Anthony Seibold, but on Saturday felt he was ready to take on premiership frontrunners Penrith. “He’s got endless natural ability,” Foran said in his pre-game media conference. “On top of that, he is a wonderful student of the game, he works extremely hard. He is a tough kid and is really courageous and competitive.



Related Article NRL 2026 Has the need for speed turned the NRL into touch footy? These numbers suggest otherwise “He just ticks so many boxes. Without putting too much pressure on him, we have high hopes for Joey’s future in this game. We love what he is about. “And tomorrow night he gets to go out there and do it. And we have all the belief in the world he is going to get out there and get the job done.” One of Walsh’s idols growing up was Daly Cherry-Evans. The youngster said he was fortunate to spend time with the former Manly captain while they are both at the club. “I learned loads, he was unreal to me,” Walsh said. “He spent lots of time helping me improve my game, obviously because it was my first year coming back to league.



“He’s taught me to keep playing eyes-up footy, the structure and all that will come with games, but just try and keep your eyes up and play with your instincts, which was a very good lesson.” With AAP

World.title: Nepean byelection LIVE: Liberal Party fight to retain seat as One Nation mounts challenge
World.content:
Although Sam Groth is absent from the booths today, many of his former Liberal colleagues have made the trip to Nepean to support their candidate, Anthony Marsh.

Among them are party leader Jess Wilson, deputy David Southwick, opposition education spokesperson Brad Rowswell and MP Moira Deeming, who last month gained preselection as the party’s lead candidate for the Western Metropolitan Region in the upper house. The group recently took a “family photo” outside the Rosebud Sea Scouts Hall.

Former opposition leader Brad Battin (left), Opposition Leader Jess Wilson and Liberal candidate Anthony Marsh. Wayne Taylor

Wilson said her party was not taking the seat, which has been occupied by the Liberals for 36 of the past 40 years, for granted.

“That’s why Anthony’s been down here for weeks on end, and I’ve been with him knocking on doors,” she said. “We’ve been out listening to the community, and we’ve put forward a really positive plan for the electorate.”

Wilson said voters felt neglected by Labor and that this was evidenced by the party’s decision to not stand a candidate.

“That just shows how much they don’t care about the people on the peninsula,” she said. “But me, as a future premier of Victoria, I will make sure that they get the investment down here that they deserve.”

World.title: Since the 1960s, Denis has framed his customers’ treasures: snake skins, wedding dresses and golden underpants
World.content:
Denis Kosnar, who has framed Melburnians’ lives since he was a boy.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Denis Kosnar is wrangling a 2.6-metre python skin, unfurling the great rolled-up beast and flattening it with clamps and weights. Applying snake oil to one side (or, more accurately, glycerin) and rubbing alcohol to the other, he’s been meticulously working to preserve the skin, some weeks after a woman walked into his shop and pulled it out of her bag. Her relative shot and killed it in Sri Lanka 20 years ago, she said. Denis Kosnar in his quaint and curious Kosnar’s Picture Framing and Mirrors Shop. Jason South Kosnar has been a framer for 61 years – but this is a first. “See, there are the creases there,” he says, tracing a finger over the snake’s scales through his phone screen, “we’re starting to get rid of them.” Seventy-three years ago, his father, John (Jan) Kosnar, started the family framing business, working out of a small shed at Ferny Creek in the Dandenong Ranges.



A Czechoslovakian migrant, he brought over picture framing and gilding skills. Soon enough, 14-year-old Denis was apprenticed in their new shop in Moonee Ponds in Melbourne’s north-west – the family’s first major commercial move. At one time, Kosnar’s supplied most picture framers in Australia and New Zealand, and John was formally recognised as the founder of Australia’s industry for picture frame mouldings (individual frame pieces that are cut to size). A factory and dozens of employees (85, at its height) came and went – before financial troubles in the 1990s forced the business to scale back. What’s left today are two workshops, and a quaint storefront in Ascot Vale, a suburb over from where Kosnar, 75, started. Ye olde signage covers the corner shop’s exterior, proudly declaring “Kosnar’s” from all angles. The bell chimes when you pull on the door’s great, golden handle, and inside, Julie – who has worked for the business a decade – uses a ruler and a cardboard pricing chart (dated 1993) to calculate quotes. There’s no computerising of customer orders here (Kosnar reasons that paper records can go back longer, as computer programs change and documents are lost). Thick record books are instead stuffed into shelving in a back room cluttered with hangers, screws, brackets, glues, tools and a small workbench. “When I first came to work here, it was like walking into Dickens,” Julie says, speaking over soft classical music. She waves off a request to publish her surname, insisting she stays “under the radar”.



Hand-constructed ornate frames and mirrors, many gilded by Denis, take up most of the shop’s surfaces, except for a sliver of red carpet. “We frame an awful lot of things,” Julie says. “You’d be surprised.” There was the wedding dress – a big tulle gown with a beaded bodice and empire waist – and last year, a woman came in with a full-face medical mask, with holes cut into it for the eyes. She was in remission after wearing it during cancer treatment. Julie defers to Kosnar, who brings up those golden underpants they put in a showcase frame a few years ago. “It was a prize for doing something,” he says, “but it’s probably best not to be known what it was for.” For all Kosnar’s years, he can’t choose a favourite project (to do so would be like “choosing a favourite child”) – and Kosnar’s are still not Melbourne’s oldest framers. That title belongs to Jarman, the cavernous counterpart to Kosnar’s curiosity, acquired by artists’ services company Chapman and Bailey in 2014. Founded in 1879 by John Thallon and his brother Thomas, the combined business today operates out of a Willy Wonka-style, multistorey building in Abbotsford in Melbourne’s inner north.



The showroom and gallery is merely the taster before the gilding room, the ornamental room, the mounting room, and the spraying room, where a metres-high curtain of water filters out excess paint. Chapman and Bailey’s Ying Huang is among Australia’s last ornamental specialists using traditional framing techniques. Joe Armao The Jarmans are long gone from the business, but the framers’ legacy remains, particularly in ornamental specialist Ying Huang. Beneath hodgepodge plants and old window mounts hung from the ceiling, she cooks up composite in heavy metal pots, before pressing the material into hand-cast ornamental moulds – the main attraction for owner Mark Chapman, who bought Jarman to keep the practice alive. Huang trained under Tom Whitfield, the last of Jarman Framing’s original ornamental specialists, before he retired in 2020. Nowadays, Jarman stocks a frame dubbed the “Tom special”. “One day I’ll have a frame in my name,” Huang says. On the showroom floor, clientele clearly see the value in Jarman’s craft. Two consultants – one, in a tweed vest with thick, black-rimmed glasses – cling to the side of a suited gentleman, who is weighing up framing options for an oil painting on a video call to his wife. The priciest frames here – all of which are museum-quality – can cost up to $30,000. At Kosnar’s, the maximum price is more like $8000. But when I ask Kosnar what the most valuable item they’ve framed is, his answer isn’t monetary.

World.title: Fuel spike is coming: Relief at bowser not tipped to last
World.content:
The cost of petrol and diesel is set to climb again in coming weeks after Australia’s regional oil prices hit a new wartime high, piling pressure on the federal government to extend its 26¢ cut to the fuel excise beyond the June 30 deadline. Motorists have enjoyed a two-week window of relief at the pump after the US-Iran ceasefire raised hopes of an imminent end to the conflict, spurring a swift fall in crude oil and fuel prices. Fuel prices are set to rise. Louie Douvis But as a series of peace talks foundered, crushing prospects of Middle East energy exports returning to normal any time soon, benchmark oil prices have risen to their highest levels since Iran all but closed the Strait of Hormuz on February 28. On Friday, Australia’s regional oil benchmark, Tapis crude, was trading at $US125 ($174) a barrel, its highest mark since the global energy crisis sparked by the war in Ukraine in 2022, and almost double the $US65 price point underpinning the Australian government’s mid-year budget update.



While prices dropped slightly on overseas markets overnight, international oil bosses are sounding the alarm as stockpiles run down. “A lot of the inventory and spare capacity has been depleted already,” Chevron chief financial officer Eimear Bonner told Bloomberg. “There’s very little of the buffer left.” “The market hasn’t seen the full impact of that yet,” Exxon chief executive Darren Woods told analysts overnight. “There’s more to come if the strait remains closed.” “Markets are not liking what is happening in the Middle East,” said Peter Khoury, a spokesman for the National Roads and Motorists Association. Related Article Visual story

Oil If Australia’s greener than ever, how much oil do we really need? The reality is brutal



Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Friday that economic damage from the war would have a “long tail to it”. “We don’t know when this war will end. We don’t know what the consequences will be. We don’t know if the Strait of Hormuz will be open, what the timeframe is, and we know that even if it opened tomorrow,” Albanese said. Albanese has not ruled out extending the fuel excise cut beyond June, and said last month that the government would “examine it at an appropriate time”. Treasurer Jim Chalmers has emphasised the role the cut has played in driving down prices since April, after a 33 per cent jump in petrol prices helped push inflation to 4.6 per cent in March. “This shows how important and how necessary that decision from the government was since we halved the fuel excise,” he said on Wednesday.



While Sydney and Melbourne drivers saw regular unleaded averaging $1.80 and diesel at $2.50 a litre on Friday, those figures are expected to jump within seven to 10 days’ time as the international spike filters through to local service stations. In late March, diesel prices hit a high of $3.10 a litre, while unleaded petrol rose to $2.59 a litre. While price spikes are imminent, pressure on the local fuel supply chain has eased. Previously unpublished government data reveals that panic buying has subsided as petrol and diesel sales have returned to typical levels, after consumption hit a high point in the first week of March. Fuel excise volumes – a key indicator of how much fuel has been sold in the nation as it is charged per litre – surged to a six-year peak in the weeks following February 28, when US President Donald Trump launched his attack on Iran. The spike was driven by a wave of panic buying as motorists and businesses braced for the risk of major price hikes and supply shortfalls.



Related Article Inside Story

Energy Scott was already working late on fuel supply when a call stopped him cold However, demand has plummeted by as much as 20 per cent since early March, signalling that motorists are changing their driving behaviour. Prices have eased and supply has increased since fuel importers procured additional cargoes in March and the government secured agreements with Asian fuel exporters to shore up supply. The number of local service stations without fuel has fallen to less than half the number recorded during the first weeks of the war. Experts attribute the massive fall in fuel demand to people changing their driving behaviour to deal with higher prices, as well as the impact of increased government and industry messaging encouraging motorists to adopt fuel-saving measures, take public transport where possible, and not fill up unnecessarily.



“I would suggest it’s all of the above,” Khoury said. “Sustained periods of really high prices result in people driving less, combining trips and using public transport more.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Tiwai Point aluminium smelter workers announce strike
World.content:
Photo: RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Workers at the Tiwai Point aluminium smelter have voted to take industrial action from Monday, following unsuccessful bargaining, but the smelter - owned by Rio Tinto, says it provides a competitive package.

E tū union members at New Zealand's Aluminium Smelter in Southland, owned by Rio Tinto, have been in bargaining since 2024.

E tū Director Mat Danaher told RNZ the dispute was about the basic right of working people to organise.

"We believe this failure to agree is a deliberate anti-union tactic," he said.

"They do not want to have a collective employment agreement in place. It feels like they would much prefer workers to continue to be individuals who they can push around and kind of decide what they want to do and basically deny the workers the right to a voice."

Danaher said Rio Tinto had a track record of anti-union behaviour, with workers in Australia having also taken industrial action.

He added that industrial action was a last resort, but Rio Tinto needed to understand Tiwai Point aluminium smelter workers could not be taken for granted.

"This is a hugely profitable global company," Danaher said.

"It reported underlying EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation) of $US25.4 billion ($NZ43bn) and profit after tax of $US10bn ($NZ17bn) for 2025, and announced ordinary dividends of $US6.5bn (NZ$11bn).

"The workers who keep Tiwai running deserve a fair share of that success."

Delegate and production worker Dee said workers had not asked for anything excessive.

"We're not being unreasonable. What we want is decent work. We want an agreement that recognises the job we do, the conditions we work under, and the contribution we make."

In a statement, Rio Tinto said New Zealand's Aluminium Smelter believed that the terms and conditions it offered were competitive.

A spokesperson said it positioned the organisation well, both in the Southland and wider New Zealand market.

"We will continue to engage with the union, and all our staff, in good faith and have confirmed we will recommence mediation on 20 May."

The spokesperson said New Zealand's Aluminium Smelter's priorities were "safety and environmental stewardship, and stability of our operations and of our local communities".

"In a tough economic environment for many businesses, we're proud to continue to offer our team members and those looking to join our team market leading benefits and we will continue to do so as part of Tiwai continuing to be a great place to work."

Around 185 E tū members are expected to take industrial action on 4, 6, 8, and 10 May.
